Identify the part of the sentence that contains an error. Choose (E) if there is no error.

(A) The manager, along with his team members,
(B) were present
(C) at the meeting
(D) yesterday.
With 'along with', the verb agrees with the singular subject 'the manager', so 'was present' is correct.

Identify the part of the sentence that contains an error. Choose (E) if there is no error.

(A) Each of the students
(B) have submitted
(C) the assignment
(D) on time.

Identify the part of the sentence that contains an error. Choose (E) if there is no error.

(A) Neither the principal
(B) nor the teachers
(C) was aware
(D) of the change.
With 'neither ... nor', the verb agrees with the nearer subject 'teachers', so 'were aware' is correct.

Identify the part of the sentence that contains an error. Choose (E) if there is no error.

(A) She has been working
(B) in this bank
(C) since five years
(D) without a break.
'Since' is used with a point of time; with a duration such as 'five years', 'for' is required.

Identify the part of the sentence that contains an error. Choose (E) if there is no error.

(A) Hardly had the train
(B) left the platform
(C) than it started
(D) raining.
'Hardly ... when' is the correct pair; 'than' is used with 'no sooner'.

Identify the part of the sentence that contains an error. Choose (E) if there is no error.

(A) No sooner had she
(B) entered the room
(C) when the phone
(D) rang.
'No sooner ... than' is the fixed correlative pair, so 'than the phone rang' is correct.

Identify the part of the sentence that contains an error. Choose (E) if there is no error.

(A) The book,
(B) which was published last year,
(C) have become
(D) a bestseller.
The subject 'the book' is singular, so 'has become' is correct.

Identify the part of the sentence that contains an error. Choose (E) if there is no error.

(A) One of the reasons
(B) for his failure
(C) were
(D) his careless attitude.
The subject is 'one', which is singular, so 'was' is correct.

Identify the part of the sentence that contains an error. Choose (E) if there is no error.

(A) The teacher asked
(B) the students
(C) to read the chapter
(D) careful.
'Read' is a verb and needs the adverb 'carefully'.

Identify the part of the sentence that contains an error. Choose (E) if there is no error.

(A) He is one of the few candidates
(B) who
(C) has cleared
(D) the interview.
'Who' refers to the plural 'candidates', so 'have cleared' is correct.

Identify the part of the sentence that contains an error. Choose (E) if there is no error.

(A) The company's profits
(B) has increased
(C) significantly
(D) over the past year.
'Profits' is plural, so it takes 'have increased'.

Identify the part of the sentence that contains an error. Choose (E) if there is no error.

(A) The chairman and the secretary
(B) is attending
(C) the conference
(D) in Delhi.
Two subjects joined by 'and' take a plural verb, so 'are attending' is correct.

Identify the part of the sentence that contains an error. Choose (E) if there is no error.

(A) Neither of the two proposals
(B) were accepted
(C) by the committee
(D) at the meeting.
'Neither of' is singular and takes 'was accepted'.

Identify the part of the sentence that contains an error. Choose (E) if there is no error.

(A) The number of applicants
(B) have risen
(C) sharply
(D) this year.
'The number of' takes a singular verb, so 'has risen' is correct.

Identify the part of the sentence that contains an error. Choose (E) if there is no error.

(A) A large number of students
(B) was absent
(C) from the class
(D) yesterday.
'A large number of' takes a plural verb, so 'were absent' is correct.

Identify the part of the sentence that contains an error. Choose (E) if there is no error.

(A) The furniture
(B) in the new office
(C) are
(D) very expensive.
'Furniture' is an uncountable singular noun, so it takes 'is'.

Identify the part of the sentence that contains an error. Choose (E) if there is no error.

(A) She gave me
(B) a useful advice
(C) before
(D) the interview.
'Advice' is uncountable and cannot take the article 'a'.

Identify the part of the sentence that contains an error. Choose (E) if there is no error.

(A) He has
(B) many informations
(C) about
(D) the new scheme.
'Information' is uncountable, so 'much information' is correct.

Identify the part of the sentence that contains an error. Choose (E) if there is no error.

(A) The scenery
(B) of the hill station
(C) were
(D) breathtaking.
'Scenery' is an uncountable singular noun and takes 'was'.

Identify the part of the sentence that contains an error. Choose (E) if there is no error.

(A) I prefer
(B) coffee
(C) than tea
(D) in the morning.
'Prefer' is followed by 'to', not 'than': 'prefer coffee to tea'.

Identify the part of the sentence that contains an error. Choose (E) if there is no error.

(A) She is
(B) senior
(C) than me
(D) by two years.
Latin comparatives such as 'senior' take 'to', not 'than'.

Identify the part of the sentence that contains an error. Choose (E) if there is no error.

(A) The teacher was
(B) angry on
(C) the students
(D) for their negligence.
'Angry with' is used for people, while 'angry at' is used for things.

Identify the part of the sentence that contains an error. Choose (E) if there is no error.

(A) She insisted
(B) to come along
(C) with us
(D) to the market.
'Insist' is followed by 'on' and a gerund, so 'insisted on coming' is correct.

Identify the part of the sentence that contains an error. Choose (E) if there is no error.

(A) The doctor advised me
(B) to not eat
(C) junk food
(D) at night.
In the infinitive, 'not' precedes 'to': 'advised me not to eat'.

Identify the part of the sentence that contains an error. Choose (E) if there is no error.

(A) Being a rainy day,
(B) we decided
(C) to stay
(D) indoors.
The participial phrase must refer to the subject 'we', but 'we' were not a rainy day. It should read 'It being a rainy day, we decided ...'.

Identify the part of the sentence that contains an error. Choose (E) if there is no error.

(A) Walking down the street,
(B) a strange sight
(C) caught
(D) my attention.
The participle 'walking' should refer to the person, not the sight. It should read 'As I was walking down the street, a strange sight caught my attention'.

Identify the part of the sentence that contains an error. Choose (E) if there is no error.

(A) He not only lost
(B) his wallet
(C) but also
(D) his passport.
'Not only' should be placed before the object it parallels: 'lost not only his wallet but also his passport'.

Identify the part of the sentence that contains an error. Choose (E) if there is no error.

(A) The two sisters
(B) quarrelled
(C) with one another
(D) over a trivial matter.
'Each other' is used for two people, while 'one another' is used for more than two.

Identify the part of the sentence that contains an error. Choose (E) if there is no error.

(A) The committee has taken
(B) its decision
(C) and they will announce
(D) it soon.
'The committee' is treated as singular here ('its'), so the pronoun should be 'it will announce'.

Identify the part of the sentence that contains an error. Choose (E) if there is no error.

(A) The reason why
(B) he failed
(C) is because
(D) he did not study.
'The reason ... is that' is the correct structure; 'is because' is redundant after 'the reason'.

Identify the part of the sentence that contains an error. Choose (E) if there is no error.

(A) He is
(B) enough strong
(C) to lift the box
(D) alone.
'Enough' follows the adjective, so 'strong enough' is correct.

Identify the part of the sentence that contains an error. Choose (E) if there is no error.

(A) I am looking forward
(B) to meet you
(C) at the conference
(D) next week.
'Look forward to' is followed by a gerund, so 'to meeting you' is correct.

Identify the part of the sentence that contains an error. Choose (E) if there is no error.

(A) She has been living
(B) in this city
(C) for the last ten years
(D) and enjoys it thoroughly.
The present perfect continuous 'has been living' correctly pairs with 'for the last ten years', and 'enjoys' agrees with 'she'.

Identify the part of the sentence that contains an error. Choose (E) if there is no error.

(A) The report,
(B) along with the annexures,
(C) was submitted
(D) on time.
The singular subject 'the report' correctly takes 'was', and the remaining parts are error-free.

Identify the part of the sentence that contains an error. Choose (E) if there is no error.

(A) Neither the manager
(B) nor the employees
(C) were available
(D) for comment.
With 'neither ... nor', the verb agrees with the nearer plural subject 'employees', so 'were' is correct.

Identify the part of the sentence that contains an error. Choose (E) if there is no error.

(A) Hardly had we reached
(B) the station
(C) when the train
(D) departed.
'Hardly ... when' is correctly used, and the past perfect 'had reached' matches 'departed'.

Identify the part of the sentence that contains an error. Choose (E) if there is no error.

(A) The teacher asked
(B) the students
(C) to read the chapter
(D) carefully.
The adverb 'carefully' correctly modifies the verb 'read'.

Identify the part of the sentence that contains an error. Choose (E) if there is no error.

(A) A number of issues
(B) were raised
(C) at the meeting
(D) yesterday.
'A number of' takes a plural verb, so 'were raised' is correct.

Identify the part of the sentence that contains an error. Choose (E) if there is no error.

(A) The information
(B) provided by the witness
(C) was extremely
(D) useful.
'Information' is uncountable and singular, so 'was' is correct.

Identify the part of the sentence that contains an error. Choose (E) if there is no error.

(A) She prefers
(B) tea
(C) to coffee
(D) in the morning.
'Prefer ... to ...' is the correct structure, and all other parts are error-free.
